entities.summary:
Áed mac Néill, commonly called Áed Oirdnide, was a prominent Irish monarch who ruled during the early Medieval period. A member of the prestigious Cenél nEógain dynasty of the northern Uí Néill, he was the son of Niall Frossach, whose own legacy shaped the political landscape of Early Medieval Ireland. Like his father, Áed was reckoned among the High Kings of Ireland, a title reflecting his supreme authority and influence across the island.

Aed's reign marked a significant period in Medieval Irish history, characterized by the consolidation of dynastic power and territorial authority. He ascended to the kingship of Ailech in 788 CE and subsequently rose to the position of High King of Ireland in 797 CE, maintaining this elevated status until his death in 819 CE. His tenure as ruler embodied the interplay of religious authority, feudal governance structures, and the expansion of trade networks that defined the Medieval era.

As a sovereign authority within the framework of Monarchs and Rulers, Áed Oirdnide played a crucial role in establishing dynastic legacies and territorial boundaries that would influence Irish political structures for generations to come. His rule during the transition period of the early ninth century witnessed the complex interactions between secular power and ecclesiastical influence that characterized Medieval Ireland. The frameworks governing his reign—encompassing political systems, empire and colonial expansion, and geopolitical linkage—reflect the sophisticated mechanisms of medieval governance and international relations of his time.
